question: A 29-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of a 10-day history of small quantities of intermittent, blood-tinged discharge from her left nipple. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 5 years. Her last menstrual period was 12 days ago. She is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently. Physical examination shows scant serosanguinous fluid expressible from the left nipple. There is no palpable breast mass or axillary lymphadenopathy. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.opb: Image-guided core biopsy of the affected duct

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "29-year-old woman with blood-tinged nipple discharge" -> "possible causes include benign or malignant conditions" -> "no palpable mass or lymphadenopathy noted" -> "serosanguinous fluid suggests possible benign etiology" -> "nipple discharge cytology can help evaluate for malignancy" -> "considering the patient's age and presentation" -> "nipple discharge cytology is the most appropriate next step" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Patient has blood-tinged discharge from left nipple" -> "10-day history suggests ongoing issue" -> "no significant findings on physical examination" -> "risk factors include smoking and inconsistent condom use" -> "nipple discharge cytology is a non-invasive test" -> "can provide information on cellular abnormalities" -> "considered appropriate next step" -> 75%

CHAIN: "Blood-tinged discharge in a young woman" -> "no mass or lymphadenopathy found" -> "serosanguinous fluid suggests benign causes" -> "nipple discharge cytology can help assess for cancer" -> "other imaging options may be more invasive" -> "cytology is a reasonable first step" -> 70%
analysis: The patient presents with intermittent blood-tinged discharge from the left nipple without any palpable mass or lymphadenopathy. Given her age and the nature of the discharge, the most appropriate next step is to evaluate the cause of the discharge. Nipple discharge cytology can help assess for any malignant cells or other abnormalities. While imaging studies like ultrasound can be useful, they are typically not the first step in the evaluation of nipple discharge unless there is a palpable mass. Therefore, nipple discharge cytology is the most appropriate next step.
